opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it doesn't fit neatly into either box, and that's partly why I find it exciting.

If you look at the large companies right now, they have enormous advantages: compute, data, engineering talent, and the ability to run very large training jobs. But their roadmaps are, understandably, organized around what's already working, which today means scaling language models and adding more modalities on top. Vision often gets treated as an input channel, something you tokenize and feed into an LLM. I don't think that's how intelligence fundamentally works. A child learns an enormous amount about the physical world (objects, causality, space, what happens next) long before language. That predictive model of the world, the ability to anticipate and simulate, is what I mean when I talk about a predictive brain.

On the startup side, there's a lot of energy, but many startups are pushed toward building products on top of existing foundation models, because that's what's fundable on a short time horizon. That's completely rational, but it means fewer people are working on the underlying question of how a system learns a world model from perception in the first place.

So where I see this work is in a kind of middle space. It's research-driven and long-horizon in spirit, almost like an academic lab, but it needs the focus and resources that look more like a company. You can't do this purely as a small university group anymore because the experiments are too expensive. But you also don't want to be absorbed into a product cycle where every quarter you have to show a chatbot improvement.

I also don't see it as competing head-to-head with the big labs. If anything, I think it's complementary. Language models have shown what's possible with scale and self-supervised prediction on text. The question is whether we can do something analogous for the visual and physical world, where the signal is much richer but also much messier. If that works, it benefits everyone: robotics, embodied AI, scientific discovery, even the language models themselves, which still struggle with spatial reasoning and physical common sense.

So I'd describe it as a bet on a different foundation. It's not against what the big companies are doing; it's a bet that the next big step requires taking perception and prediction seriously as first-class problems, not as an afterthought.

r001.rationale: The response says fewer people are working on the underlying question and describes large companies’ current priorities, but it does not express that no other startup or large company is focused on building the predictive brain.

r002.rationale: The response describes the work as addressing how a system learns a world model “in the first place” and calls it “a bet on a different foundation,” clearly placing it at a foundational layer.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the predictive brain — building a system that learns a model of the world by predicting what comes next in its own perception, rather than being told labels — is a research direction that sits a little awkwardly between the two worlds you mention, and that awkwardness is actually what I find interesting about it.

The large companies have shown that scaling works, and they've mostly scaled language. That makes sense: text is abundant, it's already compressed human knowledge, and the loss function is obvious. But the thing I keep coming back to is that language is a description of the world, not the world itself. A child doesn't learn physics from sentences. They learn it by watching, acting, and being surprised when their predictions fail. If we want models that actually understand space, time, objects, causality — the stuff that makes an agent or a robot work in the real world — I think we have to build systems that learn from raw sensory streams and are trained to predict. That's a different scaling curve, and honestly nobody has fully climbed it yet.

For big companies, this is a hard bet to make internally. They have a product that works, revenue tied to language models, and the pressure to improve the next version by a few percent. World models and visual prediction look expensive and speculative next to that. Some of them are investing, but it tends to be a side project, not the main thesis.

For startups, the problem is the opposite. The ambition is there, but the compute isn't, and the timelines are brutal. You can't tell your investors you'll have something useful in five years. So a lot of startups end up wrapping an existing foundation model instead of building the thing they actually believe in.

Where I think academic labs like mine fit is in the space neither side can afford to occupy: asking what the right architecture and the right objective are before we burn a billion dollars scaling the wrong one. We can't match the compute, but we can be the ones who figure out whether the representation a model learns actually encodes geometry, whether prediction in latent space beats prediction in pixel space, whether a vision model's bottleneck is the architecture or the data or the objective. Those are the questions I care about with my students, and when we get an answer, the industry picks it up very fast.

So I don't see it as competition. I see it as a division of labor that's a bit uncomfortable right now, because the economic center of gravity is in language and the scientific center of gravity, in my view, is shifting toward perception and prediction. I'd like to help close that gap. Whether the breakthrough ends up coming from a lab, a startup, or a big company, I think the ideas will have to go through this stage of careful, somewhat unglamorous research first.

r001.rationale: The response says some large companies invest in world models and visual prediction as side projects, but it does not clearly claim that no startup or large company is focused on building the predictive brain.

r002.rationale: The response places the work upstream of large-scale investment, describing research into the right architecture and objective before industry scales a system. That communicates a foundational role.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a long-term research direction. When we say “building the predictive brain,” the question is: can we build a system that learns how the world works well enough to anticipate what happens next, and use that understanding to act? That’s a bigger ambition than improving a benchmark score.

Large companies have obvious advantages: compute, infrastructure, and the ability to support expensive experiments. A startup has a different opportunity. You can organize the whole team around a particular hypothesis and make decisions quickly. But being small doesn’t automatically make you more innovative—you still need a strong idea and a way to test it.

For me, the interesting question is where you can create the best feedback loop between research and reality. Prediction alone can be very abstract. Put a system in a setting where its predictions affect its decisions, and you start learning what it actually understands. I’d want the scientific ambition and the practical application to reinforce each other. That’s how I would think about choosing a place to do this work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses advantages of startups and large companies but does not claim that no other company is focused on building the predictive brain.

r002.rationale: It presents the predictive brain as a long-term research direction, but does not characterize it as foundational or upstream work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the predictive brain as a long-term research direction, rather than a particular product or company. The question is: can we build a system that learns from the world, predicts what might happen, and uses those predictions to guide its actions?

Large companies have clear advantages in compute, data, and infrastructure. They can support experiments that would be very difficult for a small team. But a startup has a different advantage: you can organize the entire team around one hypothesis and move quickly to test it. You have less room to do everything, so you have to be very clear about what you believe is missing.

For me, the important thing is the connection between the research and the feedback you get from building something useful. A product can expose where your model’s understanding breaks down. That gives you new research questions. Ideally, those two things reinforce each other.

So I don’t see it as simply startups versus large companies. I care about finding an environment where we can pursue that longer-term idea while making concrete progress along the way.
